title: The Botanist Who Ended Ireland's Famine Cycle
event_summary: Scottish botanist Robert Fortune, disguised as a Chinese merchant, successfully smuggled 20,000 tea plants and expert Chinese tea workers out of China's Fujian province to British-controlled Darjeeling and Assam. This act of industrial espionage shattered China's centuries-old monopoly on tea production, redirecting enormous flows of silver that had been draining the British treasury. Within a decade, Indian tea surpassed Chinese exports, fundamentally restructuring the global economy.
why_forgotten: The British East India Company actively obscured Fortune's espionage because it exposed the empire's willingness to steal rather than innovate. The story also implicates the exploitation of Chinese workers who were deceived into relocating. It sits uncomfortably between celebrated botanical science and straightforward corporate theft, so neither China nor Britain had reason to publicize it.
why_it_matters: Fortune's theft created the Indian and Sri Lankan tea industries that employ millions today and made tea a global commodity rather than a Chinese luxury. More broadly, it was one of history's most consequential acts of intellectual property theft, foreshadowing modern disputes over trade secrets and biopiracy. The silver that stopped flowing to China weakened the Qing Dynasty's economy, contributing to the instability that led to the Taiping Rebellion and the eventual fall of imperial China.
